summary: Describes how an IPv4 host can detect an address conflict, where two hosts on the same link use the same address. It provides a precaution a host can take before using an address and a way to notice conflicts afterward. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If two computers on the same network end up with the same IP address, their traffic gets mixed up and connections keep dropping. This RFC tells a computer how to check that an address is free before it starts using it, and what to do if it finds the address is already taken.

questions: what is ipv4 address conflict detection
how does a host defend its ip address
subtitle: How a host checks that an IPv4 address is free before it starts using it.

tldr.problem: Two hosts on the same link configured with the same IPv4 address break each other's connections, and the DHCP specification gave no guidance on how a host should find out.
tldr.mechanism: A host broadcasts ARP probes with a zero sender address, listens for a reply or another probe for the same address, and then broadcasts announcements to say it is taking the address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC fixes the timing, the packets and what a host does when a conflict appears later, including a rate limit so a broken address server cannot cause an ARP storm.

today: RFC 5227 is a Proposed Standard from July 2008 that updates RFC 826, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not change the ARP packet format or its rules; it adds a probing and announcement step before a host starts using an address, and an ongoing check afterwards.

sections.title: The Problem and What the RFC Fixes
sections.content:
Historically, accidentally configuring two Internet hosts with the same IP address has often been an annoying and hard-to-diagnose problem. This is unfortunate, because the existing Address Resolution Protocol provides an easy way for a host to detect this kind of misconfiguration and report it to the user.

The DHCP specification briefly mentions the role of ARP in detecting misconfiguration: the client should probe the newly received address, the client should perform a final check on the parameters, and if the client detects that the address is already in use it must send a DHCPDECLINE message to the server. Unfortunately, the DHCP specification does not give any guidance to implementers concerning the number of ARP packets to send, the interval between packets, the total time to wait before concluding that an address may safely be used, or indeed even which kinds of packets a host should be listening for. It leaves unspecified the action a host should take if, after concluding that an address may safely be used, it subsequently discovers that it was wrong.

This document specifies the required actions for three things: determining whether use of an address is likely to lead to an addressing conflict, whether another host is already using it and whether two hosts are about to begin using it at the same time; subsequent passive detection that another host on the network is inadvertently using the same address; and rate-limiting of address acquisition attempts in the case of an excessive number of repeated conflicts.

The utility of address conflict detection is not limited to DHCP clients. No matter how an address was configured, whether by manual entry, from a DHCP server or by any other means, detecting conflicts is useful. Upon detecting a conflict, the configuring agent should be notified of the error: for a human user that might be an error message on a screen, an SNMP notification, or a text message to a mobile phone, and for a DHCP server it takes the form of a DHCP DECLINE message.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP told clients to check an address with ARP but not how to do the check, so every implementation invented its own. This RFC spells the check out: how many packets to send, how long to wait, what to listen for, and what to do when the address turns out to be in use.

sections.title: ARP Probe, ARP Announcement and the Timing Constants
sections.content:
An ARP Probe is an ARP Request packet, broadcast on the local link, with an all-zero sender IP address. The sender hardware address must contain the hardware address of the interface sending the packet. The sender IP address field must be set to all zeroes, to avoid polluting ARP caches in other hosts on the same link in the case where the address turns out to be already in use by another host. The target hardware address field is ignored and should be set to all zeroes, and the target IP address field must be set to the address being probed. An ARP Probe conveys both a question, is anyone using this address, and an implied statement, this is the address I hope to use.

An ARP Announcement is an ARP Request packet, broadcast on the local link, identical to the ARP Probe except that both the sender and target IP address fields contain the IP address being announced. It conveys a stronger statement, this is the address I am now using.

The timing constants are fixed values, not intended to be modifiable by implementers, operators or end users. PROBE_WAIT is 1 second, the initial random delay. PROBE_NUM is 3, the number of probe packets. PROBE_MIN is 1 second and PROBE_MAX is 2 seconds, the minimum and maximum delay until a repeated probe. ANNOUNCE_WAIT is 2 seconds, the delay before announcing. ANNOUNCE_NUM is 2, the number of announcement packets, and ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL is 2 seconds, the time between them. MAX_CONFLICTS is 10, the number of conflicts before rate-limiting, and RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL is 60 seconds, the delay between successive attempts. DEFEND_INTERVAL is 10 seconds, the minimum interval between defensive ARPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe asks whether an address is taken while claiming nothing, because the sender address field is left as zeroes. An announcement makes the claim, putting the new address in both the sender and target fields. The RFC fixes the numbers: three probes, a wait of up to a second before the first one, then two announcements two seconds apart.

sections.title: Which Networks This Applies To
sections.content:
This specification applies to all IEEE 802 local area networks, including Ethernet, Token Ring and IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, as well as to other link-layer technologies that operate at data rates of at least 1 Mb/s, have a round-trip latency of at most one second, and use ARP to map from IP addresses to link-layer hardware addresses. Link-layer technologies that support ARP but operate at lower rates or higher latencies will still work correctly with this protocol, but more often may have to handle late conflicts detected after the probing phase has completed, and may want different values for the timing constants.

For the protocol to be effective, it is not necessary that all hosts on the link implement it. For a given host implementing this specification to be protected against accidental address conflicts, all that is required is that the peers on the same link correctly implement the ARP protocol. When a peer receives an ARP Request whose target protocol address matches one of its own addresses, then as long as it responds with a correctly formatted ARP Reply, the querying host can detect that the address is already in use.

The specifications allow hosts to detect conflicts between two hosts using the same address on the same physical link. Address conflict detection does not detect conflicts between two hosts using the same address on different physical links, and it should not: the address 10.0.0.1 is in use by countless devices on countless private networks throughout the world, and that is not a conflict. Two hosts are considered to be on the same link if a unicast, multicast or broadcast packet sent from one to another arrives with the entire link-layer payload unmodified, and a broadcast sent over the link by any host can be received by every other host in the set. The link-layer header may be modified, so packets may pass through repeaters, bridges, hubs or switches and still count as being on the same link, but not through a router that changes the IP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The method works on ordinary local networks, whether wired or wireless. It does not need every machine on the network to run it: it is enough that the other machines answer ARP requests correctly. Two machines using the same address on different networks is not a conflict and is not detected.

sections.title: Probing an Address Before Use
sections.content:
Before beginning to use an IPv4 address, whether received from manual configuration, DHCP or some other means, a host implementing this specification must test to see if the address is already in use, by broadcasting ARP Probe packets. This also applies when a network interface transitions from an inactive to an active state, when a computer awakes from sleep, when a link-state change signals that an Ethernet cable has been connected, or when an 802.11 wireless interface associates with a new base station.

A host must not perform this check periodically as a matter of course, because that would waste network bandwidth and is unnecessary given the ability of hosts to passively discover conflicts.

When ready to begin probing, the host should wait for a random time interval selected uniformly in the range zero to PROBE_WAIT seconds, and then send PROBE_NUM probe packets, each spaced randomly and uniformly PROBE_MIN to PROBE_MAX seconds apart. The initial random delay helps ensure that a large number of hosts powered on at the same time do not all send their initial probe packets simultaneously.

If, during the period from the beginning of the probing process until ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the last probe packet is sent, the host receives any ARP packet, Request or Reply, on the interface where the probe is being performed, and the packet's sender IP address is the address being probed for, then the host must treat this address as being in use by some other host and should indicate to the configuring agent that the proposed address is not acceptable. The host must also treat the arrival of an ARP Probe for the same address, from a hardware address that is not one of its own, as a conflict. That check on the sender hardware address is important, because some Ethernet hubs and many wireless access points rebroadcast received broadcast packets to all recipients, including the original sender, so a host must not be confused when it sees its own ARP packets echoed back.

If, by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the transmission of the last ARP Probe, no conflicting ARP Reply or ARP Probe has been received, then the host has successfully determined that the desired address may be used safely.
sections.plainLanguage: The host waits a random moment, then sends three probes, each one to two seconds after the last. If any ARP packet arrives claiming the same address, the address is taken and the host says so. If nothing arrives, the address is free. The random delay stops a crowd of machines starting together from all probing at the same instant.

sections.title: Announcing the Address
sections.content:
Having probed to determine that a desired address may be used safely, a host implementing this specification must then announce that it is commencing to use this address by broadcasting ANNOUNCE_NUM ARP Announcements, spaced ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL seconds apart. An ARP Announcement is identical to the ARP Probe except that now the sender and target IP addresses are both set to the host's newly selected IPv4 address.

The purpose of these announcements is to make sure that other hosts on the link do not have stale ARP cache entries left over from some other host that may previously have been using the same address. The host may begin legitimately using the IP address immediately after sending the first of the two announcements, and the sending of the second may be completed asynchronously, concurrent with other networking operations the host wishes to perform.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the address looks free, the host says twice, two seconds apart, that it is now using the address. That clears out any cached mapping left over from a machine that had the address before, and the host may start sending traffic straight after the first announcement.

sections.title: Ongoing Detection and Defending the Address
sections.content:
Address conflict detection is not limited to the time of initial interface configuration. It is an ongoing process that is in effect for as long as a host is using an address. At any time, if a host receives an ARP packet, Request or Reply, where the sender IP address is one of the host's own addresses configured on that interface but the sender hardware address does not match any of the host's own interface addresses, then this is a conflicting ARP packet, indicating some other host also thinks it is validly using this address.

To resolve the conflict a host must respond in one of three ways. It may elect to immediately cease using the address and signal an error to the configuring agent. If it has active TCP connections or other reasons to prefer to keep the same address, and it has not seen any other conflicting ARP packets within the last DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, it may attempt to defend its address by recording the time the conflicting packet was received and then broadcasting one single ARP Announcement, giving its own IP and hardware addresses as the sender addresses, with the target IP address set to its own address and the target hardware address set to all zeroes. It can then continue using the address normally. However, if this is not the first conflicting ARP packet it has seen and the previous one was within DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, it must immediately cease using the address, so that two hosts do not get stuck in an endless loop both defending the same address.

A host configured such that it should not give up its address under any circumstances, perhaps because it is the kind of device that needs a well-known stable address such as a link's default router or a DNS server, may elect to defend its address indefinitely. It should log useful information such as the source Ethernet address from the ARP packet and inform an administrator, with the number of such notifications appropriately controlled. It must not send another defensive announcement if it has seen another conflicting packet within the last DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, so that two misconfigured hosts do not flood the network with broadcast traffic while both try to defend the same address.

A host wishing to provide reliable network operation must respond to conflicting ARP packets in one of these ways. Ignoring them results in seemingly random network failures that can be hard to diagnose. Forced address reconfiguration may be disruptive, causing TCP and other transport-layer connections to be broken, but such disruptions should be exceedingly rare, and if inadvertent address duplication happens then disruption of communication is inevitable. Before abandoning an address due to a conflict, hosts should actively attempt to reset any existing connections using that address.
sections.plainLanguage: Even after the address is in use, the host keeps listening. If a packet arrives claiming the host's own address from a different machine, the host has three options: give the address up, defend it once by announcing it, or, for a machine that must keep its address, keep defending it but report it to an administrator. Defending twice in quick succession is not allowed, or two machines would argue forever.

sections.title: Why Announcements Use Request Packets
sections.content:
A question asked repeatedly during the deliberations from 2000 to 2008 was whether ARP announcements should be performed using gratuitous ARP Reply packets. On the face of it this seems reasonable, since a conventional ARP Reply is an answer to a question, and if no question had been asked it would be reasonable to describe such a reply as gratuitous.

In practice there are two reasons for using ARP Request packets instead. The historical precedent is that gratuitous ARP is documented as using ARP Request packets, and BSD Unix, Microsoft Windows, Mac OS 9 and Mac OS X all use ARP Request packets as described. At this stage, trying to mandate that they all switch would be futile.

The practical reason is that ARP Request packets are more likely to work correctly with more existing ARP implementations, some of which may not implement RFC 826 entirely correctly. The opcode is the last thing checked in the packet processing rules, so it should not matter, but there are more ways that an incorrect implementation might plausibly reject an ARP Reply than an ARP Request. An incorrect implementation may expect that ARP Replies are only sent via unicast, may expect that ARP Replies are only received in response to ARP Requests it issued recently, may ignore ARP Replies where the target hardware address does not match its hardware address, or may ignore ARP Replies where the target protocol address does not match its IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: An announcement could have been sent as a reply, but replies are the part of ARP that implementations most often get wrong. Requests are the part they expect to see arriving on their own, so sending the announcement as a request is the safer choice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPv4 address conflict detection is based on ARP and inherits the security vulnerabilities of that protocol. A malicious host may send fraudulent ARP packets on the network, interfering with the correct operation of other hosts. For example, it is easy for a host to answer all ARP Requests with Replies giving its own hardware address, thereby claiming ownership of every address on the network.

This specification makes this existing ARP vulnerability no worse, and in some ways makes it better: instead of failing silently with no indication why, hosts implementing this specification either attempt to reconfigure automatically, or at least inform the human user of what is happening. If a host willingly selects a new address in response to an ARP conflict, this potentially makes it easier for malicious attackers on the same link to hijack TCP connections. Having a host actively reset any existing connections before abandoning an address helps mitigate this risk.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP has never been secure against a machine on the same wire that lies about who owns an address. This RFC does not fix that, but it does mean the clash is noticed and reported instead of causing silent failures.

viz.caption: THE TIMING CONSTANTS AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: Timing constants
data.code:
PROBE_WAIT           1 second   (initial random delay)
PROBE_NUM            3          (number of probe packets)
PROBE_MIN            1 second   (minimum delay until repeated probe)
PROBE_MAX            2 seconds  (maximum delay until repeated probe)
ANNOUNCE_WAIT        2 seconds  (delay before announcing)
ANNOUNCE_NUM         2          (number of Announcement packets)
ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL    2 seconds  (time between Announcement packets)
MAX_CONFLICTS       10          (max conflicts before rate-limiting)
RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL 60 seconds  (delay between successive attempts)
DEFEND_INTERVAL     10 seconds  (minimum interval between defensive ARPs)

viz.caption: AN ARP PROBE AGAINST AN ARP ANNOUNCEMENT

cells: This is the address I am now using.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A HOST MAY ANSWER A CONFLICTING ARP PACKET

items.title: Give up the address
items.text: Stop using it at once and tell the configuring agent, such as the DHCP server or the operator.

items.title: Defend it once
items.text: Broadcast one announcement and carry on, unless another conflicting packet arrived within the defend interval, in which case give the address up.

items.title: Defend it indefinitely
items.text: For a device that must keep its address, keep announcing it and tell an administrator, but never announce twice within the defend interval.
